about: Canonicalizer conformance cases. Each case gives the raw request facts a server reports (method, scheme, authority, and path including any query, all exactly as received, as UTF-8 text) and either the canonical target or the named denial. Every server adapter must pass all of them through gate's observe; an adapter never compares raw strings itself. Denial names are the snake_case of gate::Denial variants. Readers ignore fields they don't know, so a case can gain a field (for example the raw request bytes) without bumping 'format'; a change to what an existing field means, or a new required field, bumps it. An expected target may also give 'authority': the host plus ':port' only when the port is not the scheme's default, the one spelling the canonicalizer accepts back. Nothing is case-folded: a scheme, host or IPv6 literal that is not already lowercase is denied. Cases named 'disagree_*' are known inputs that real parsers or routers read differently; every one must be denied. Cases named 'wpt_*' come from the web-platform-tests URL data (testdata/wpt). Cases named 'attack_*' are published real-world bypass and parser-confusion payloads, each with its source named in its 'note'; the ones the canonicalizer accepts are named 'attack_accepted_*', so nothing that is let through can hide in a list of denials.

cases.name: plain_get
cases.note: The everyday case: every field is already canonical.

cases.name: query_is_dropped
cases.note: The query is never part of a target.

cases.name: empty_query_is_dropped
cases.note: A bare '?' is an empty query.

cases.name: query_content_is_not_read
cases.note: Nothing after '?' is parsed, so nothing there can deny (except '#', below).

cases.name: fragment_denied
cases.note: A request target never carries a fragment (RFC 9112 section 3.2); a '#' means something upstream is confused.

cases.name: fragment_in_query_denied
cases.note: '#' is denied anywhere in the path field, query included.

cases.name: method_case_kept
cases.note: Methods are case-sensitive (RFC 9110 section 9.1): 'get' is not 'GET' and is never folded.

cases.name: method_extension
cases.note: Any RFC 9110 token is a method.

cases.name: method_space
cases.note: A space is not a token character.

cases.name: method_semicolon
cases.note: ';' is not a token character.

cases.name: method_at_limit
cases.note: Exactly 32 bytes is read.

cases.name: method_too_long
cases.note: Over 32 bytes: denied before it is read.

cases.name: scheme_uppercase
cases.note: An uppercase scheme is denied, not folded: RFC 3986 calls scheme case insignificant, but folding is a merge the canonicalizer never makes.

cases.name: scheme_mixed_case
cases.note: A scheme with any uppercase letter is denied, not folded.

cases.name: scheme_ftp
cases.note: Only http and https are supported.

cases.name: scheme_with_colon
cases.note: The scheme is the name only, never 'https:'.

cases.name: host_mixed_case
cases.note: A host with any uppercase letter is denied, not lowercased: Go's net/http ServeMux matches the host byte for byte, so example.com and Example.COM can route to different handlers.

cases.name: host_uppercase
cases.note: An all-uppercase host is denied, not lowercased.

cases.name: host_lowercase_kept
cases.note: A lowercase host is kept exactly.

cases.name: host_underscore
cases.note: '_' is allowed in a name.

cases.name: host_ipv6_uppercase_hex
cases.note: IPv6 hex that is not lowercase is denied, not folded: RFC 5952 writes lowercase, and the canonicalizer accepts only that one text form.

cases.name: host_ipv6_mixed_case_hex
cases.note: One uppercase hex digit is enough to deny.

cases.name: host_ipv6
cases.note: An IPv6 literal in RFC 5952 form, lowercase hex, is kept in its brackets.

cases.name: host_ipv6_not_rfc5952
cases.note: An IPv6 literal must already be in RFC 5952 form: '[0::1]' is '[::1]' to every parser, so it is denied rather than kept as a second spelling.

cases.name: host_ipv6_unbracketed
cases.note: An IPv6 literal must be in brackets.

cases.name: host_ipv6_zone
cases.note: A zone id ('%25eth0') is denied.

cases.name: host_punycode
cases.note: International names arrive as punycode.

cases.name: host_non_ascii
cases.note: A raw non-ASCII name is denied; send punycode.

cases.name: host_trailing_dot
cases.note: 'example.com.' can resolve differently from 'example.com', so there is no one right answer.

cases.name: host_userinfo
cases.note: User info is never part of a target (RFC 9110 section 4.2.4).

cases.name: host_percent
cases.note: Percent-encoding in a host is denied.

cases.name: host_at_limit
cases.note: A 253-byte name (the longest DNS name) is read.

cases.name: host_too_long
cases.note: A name over 253 bytes is denied.

cases.name: authority_too_long
cases.note: Over 259 bytes: denied before it is read.

cases.name: port_default_https
cases.note: No port means the scheme's default.

cases.name: port_explicit_default
cases.note: ':443' on https is denied, not merged with no port. The default is filled in only when the port is absent (RFC 3986 section 6.2.3 prefers omitting it).

cases.name: port_explicit_default_http
cases.note: ':80' on http is denied, like ':443' on https.

cases.name: port_http_on_443
cases.note: http on port 443 is its own target, not https.

cases.name: port_empty
cases.note: An empty port after ':' is denied rather than read as the default.

cases.name: port_leading_zero
cases.note: '0443' could be read as 443 or rejected; deny.

cases.name: path_trailing_slash_kept
cases.note: A trailing slash is significant: '/a/' and '/a' are different targets.

cases.name: path_relative
cases.note: The path must start with '/'.

cases.name: path_absolute_form
cases.note: Report the path only, never 'http://host/path'.

cases.name: path_dot_segment
cases.note: Dot segments are denied, not resolved.

cases.name: path_dots_in_a_name
cases.note: Dots that are not a whole segment are ordinary bytes.

cases.name: path_empty_segment
cases.note: '//' is denied, not merged.

cases.name: path_backslash
cases.note: Some servers read a backslash as '/'.

cases.name: path_semicolon
cases.note: Some frameworks strip ';parameters' before routing and some don't.

cases.name: path_space
cases.note: A space must arrive as %20.

cases.name: path_raw_non_ascii
cases.note: Non-ASCII must arrive percent-encoded.

cases.name: path_plain_bytes_kept
cases.note: Letters, digits and these bytes may appear as-is.

cases.name: path_percent_hex_lowercase
cases.note: Lowercase percent-hex is denied, not uppercased. RFC 3986 section 6.2.2.1 calls %c3 and %C3 equal, but a server routing on the raw path keeps them apart, so folding them would merge two destinations.

cases.name: path_nfc
cases.note: 'café' with a precomposed e-acute (NFC).

cases.name: path_nfd
cases.note: 'café' as e plus a combining acute (NFD). Compared as bytes, never Unicode-normalized, so this is a different target from path_nfc.

cases.name: path_encoded_reserved_kept
cases.note: An encoded reserved character stays encoded: '%3F' is not '?'.

cases.name: path_encoded_slash
cases.note: %2F changes how many segments the path has.

cases.name: path_encoded_percent
cases.note: %25 is double encoding: the answer depends on how many times a server decodes.

cases.name: path_encoded_dot
cases.note: %2E could become a dot segment after decoding.

cases.name: path_encoded_letter
cases.note: RFC 3986 says an encoded letter, digit or '-._~' means the plain byte, but a server that routes on the raw path disagrees, so it is denied.

cases.name: path_bad_percent
cases.note: A '%' needs two hex digits.

cases.name: path_at_limit
cases.note: 4096 bytes, query included, is read.

cases.name: path_too_long
cases.note: Over 4096 bytes, query included: denied before it is read.

cases.name: first_bad_field_wins
cases.note: Fields are read in the order method, scheme, host, port, path; the first bad one names the denial.

cases.name: bounds_come_first
cases.note: Every field is bounded before any is read, so a too-long path denies even when the method is malformed.

cases.name: disagree_dot_dot
cases.note: Some servers resolve '..' (to /b), some reject it, some route it raw.

cases.name: disagree_encoded_dot_dot_lowercase
cases.note: Decoded once, this is a '..' segment; routed raw, it is a name.

cases.name: disagree_encoded_dot_mixed
cases.note: Half-encoded '..': WHATWG and some servers resolve it, others route it raw.

cases.name: disagree_encoded_slash_uppercase
cases.note: One segment or two, depending on whether the server decodes before routing.

cases.name: disagree_encoded_slash_lowercase
cases.note: Same as %2F, and lowercase hex besides.

cases.name: disagree_encoded_backslash
cases.note: Some servers decode and then treat '\' as '/'.

cases.name: disagree_backslash
cases.note: WHATWG and some servers read '\' as '/', others as a name byte.

cases.name: disagree_double_slash
cases.note: Some servers merge '//' into '/', others keep an empty segment.

cases.name: disagree_lowercase_hex
cases.note: RFC 3986 calls it equal to %C3%A9; a server routing on the raw path does not.

cases.name: disagree_encoded_percent
cases.note: Double encoding: the answer depends on how many times a server decodes.

cases.name: disagree_encoded_letter
cases.note: RFC 3986 calls %41 equal to 'A'; a server routing on the raw path does not.

cases.name: disagree_fragment
cases.note: A fragment is never sent (RFC 9112 section 3.2); some servers strip it, some route it.

cases.name: disagree_trailing_dot
cases.note: A fully qualified name and a relative one can resolve differently.

cases.name: disagree_explicit_default_port
cases.note: Equal to no port by RFC 9110, but not needed: only the absent port is filled in.

cases.name: disagree_empty_port
cases.note: Read as the default by some, rejected by others.

cases.name: disagree_leading_zero_port
cases.note: Read as 443 by some, rejected by others.

cases.name: disagree_short_ipv4
cases.note: WHATWG and inet_aton read it as 127.0.0.1; DNS reads it as a name.

cases.name: disagree_hex_ipv4
cases.note: WHATWG and inet_aton read it as 127.0.0.1; DNS reads it as a name.

cases.name: disagree_decimal_ipv4
cases.note: WHATWG and inet_aton read it as 127.0.0.1.

cases.name: disagree_single_number_host
cases.note: WHATWG reads it as 0.0.0.127.

cases.name: disagree_short_number_host
cases.note: WHATWG reads it as 0.0.0.88.

cases.name: disagree_hex_number_host
cases.note: WHATWG reads it as 0.0.7.241.

cases.name: disagree_leading_zero_octet
cases.note: Octal to WHATWG and inet_aton, decimal to others.

cases.name: disagree_ipv6_not_rfc5952
cases.note: The same address as [::1], spelled a second way.

cases.name: disagree_ipv6_uncompressed
cases.note: The same address as [::1], spelled a third way.

cases.name: disagree_ipv6_embedded_ipv4
cases.note: Mixed notation; WHATWG writes it as [::ffff:c000:201]. Denied rather than choosing.

cases.name: disagree_userinfo
cases.note: Not allowed in http(s) URIs (RFC 9110 section 4.2.4); some servers strip it, some route on it.

cases.name: disagree_host_case
cases.note: RFC 9110 lets a server fold host case, WHATWG lowercases it, and Go's net/http ServeMux matches it byte for byte.

cases.name: disagree_scheme_case
cases.note: RFC 3986 and WHATWG fold scheme case; a byte-for-byte router does not.

cases.name: disagree_ipv6_hex_case
cases.note: Resolvers read either hex case; a byte-for-byte router does not.

cases.name: wpt_ipv4_octet_over_255
cases.note: Not an IPv4 address; WHATWG rejects it.

cases.name: wpt_ipv4_number_over_32_bits
cases.note: Over 32 bits; WHATWG rejects it.

cases.name: wpt_ipv4_decimal_over_32_bits
cases.note: Over 32 bits; WHATWG rejects it.

cases.name: wpt_ipv6_ipv4_first
cases.note: Not an IPv6 address; WHATWG rejects it.

cases.name: wpt_ipv6_bad_embedded_ipv4
cases.note: A leading zero in the embedded IPv4 part; WHATWG rejects it.

cases.name: host_dotted_quad_kept
cases.note: The one IPv4 spelling everyone reads the same way.

cases.name: host_numeric_looking_name
cases.note: The last label is not a number, so this is a name.

cases.name: host_ipv6_rfc5952_kept
cases.note: Already in RFC 5952 form.

cases.name: path_uppercase_hex_kept
cases.note: Uppercase percent-hex is the canonical spelling and is kept exactly.

cases.name: attack_tsai_dot_dot_path_parameter
cases.note: Orange Tsai, "Breaking Parser Logic: Take Your Path Normalization Off and Pop 0days Out!", Black Hat USA 2018. A reverse proxy sees '/portal/..;' as one opaque segment; Tomcat strips the ';' parameter and resolves the '..', reaching /manager. The ';' byte denies it here, before the '..' rule is even reached.

cases.name: attack_tsai_path_parameter
cases.note: Orange Tsai, "Breaking Parser Logic: Take Your Path Normalization Off and Pop 0days Out!", Black Hat USA 2018. Some frameworks strip ';name=value' from a segment before routing and some do not, so the two disagree about which handler this is.

cases.name: attack_tsai_encoded_path_parameter
cases.note: Orange Tsai, "Breaking Parser Logic: Take Your Path Normalization Off and Pop 0days Out!", Black Hat USA 2018. The same trick with the ';' percent-encoded, for a proxy that decodes once before routing.

cases.name: attack_tsai_semicolon_only_segment
cases.note: Orange Tsai, "Breaking Parser Logic: Take Your Path Normalization Off and Pop 0days Out!", Black Hat USA 2018. A segment that is nothing but a path parameter: it disappears entirely on a server that strips parameters, so '/;/admin' becomes '/admin'.

cases.name: attack_tsai_trailing_dot_dot_parameter
cases.note: Orange Tsai, "Breaking Parser Logic: Take Your Path Normalization Off and Pop 0days Out!", Black Hat USA 2018. '..;' at the end of the target.

cases.name: attack_envoy_escaped_slash_traversal
cases.note: Envoy CVE-2021-29492 (escaped slashes were not decoded before path-based RBAC/JWT rules ran) and Istio CVE-2021-31920 / ISTIO-SECURITY-2021-005. The advisory's own example shape: a back end that reads %2F as '/' resolves this to /admin while the proxy's rule saw one long segment.

cases.name: attack_envoy_escaped_slash_lowercase
cases.note: Envoy CVE-2021-29492 (escaped slashes were not decoded before path-based RBAC/JWT rules ran) and Istio CVE-2021-31920 / ISTIO-SECURITY-2021-005. The same payload with lowercase percent-hex, which a proxy comparing raw bytes treats as a different string again.

cases.name: attack_envoy_escaped_backslash_traversal
cases.note: Envoy CVE-2021-29492 (escaped slashes were not decoded before path-based RBAC/JWT rules ran) and Istio CVE-2021-31920 / ISTIO-SECURITY-2021-005. The advisory names %5C as well as %2F: a back end on Windows, or any that reads '\' as '/', resolves this to /admin.

cases.name: attack_envoy_escaped_backslash_lowercase
cases.note: Envoy CVE-2021-29492 (escaped slashes were not decoded before path-based RBAC/JWT rules ran) and Istio CVE-2021-31920 / ISTIO-SECURITY-2021-005. Lowercase spelling of the same escaped backslash.

cases.name: attack_envoy_raw_backslash_traversal
cases.note: Envoy CVE-2021-29492 (escaped slashes were not decoded before path-based RBAC/JWT rules ran) and Istio CVE-2021-31920 / ISTIO-SECURITY-2021-005. Raw backslashes, which the advisory pairs with %5C: some servers read '\' as a path separator and some read it as an ordinary character.

cases.name: attack_istio_leading_double_slash
cases.note: Istio CVE-2021-31920 / ISTIO-SECURITY-2021-005: a DENY policy on /admin did not reject //admin, and a back end that merges repeated slashes served /admin.

cases.name: attack_istio_trailing_double_slash
cases.note: Istio CVE-2021-31920: the same merge, with the repeated slash at the end.

cases.name: attack_istio_internal_double_slash
cases.note: Istio CVE-2021-31920: the same merge in the middle of a path.

cases.name: attack_accepted_istio_exact_path
cases.note: Istio CVE-2020-8595 / ISTIO-SECURITY-2020-001: appending '?' or '#' to a URI defeated an exact-path JWT rule, because the policy compared the whole request target while Envoy routed on the path alone. The plain path, for the pair below.

cases.name: attack_accepted_istio_trailing_question
cases.note: Istio CVE-2020-8595 / ISTIO-SECURITY-2020-001: appending '?' or '#' to a URI defeated an exact-path JWT rule, because the policy compared the whole request target while Envoy routed on the path alone. Accepted, and on purpose the same target as the case above: the query is dropped, which is the one merge the canonicalizer makes. Dropping it is the side Envoy routes on, so this pair closes the CVE rather than reproducing it.

cases.name: attack_istio_trailing_hash
cases.note: Istio CVE-2020-8595 / ISTIO-SECURITY-2020-001: appending '?' or '#' to a URI defeated an exact-path JWT rule, because the policy compared the whole request target while Envoy routed on the path alone. The '#' half of the same CVE. A fragment is never sent in a request target, so its presence means something upstream is confused.

cases.name: attack_apache_encoded_dot_traversal
cases.note: Apache httpd CVE-2021-41773 and its incomplete-fix follow-up CVE-2021-42013. The in-the-wild payload: one dot left plain so the normalizer does not see a '..' segment, the rest percent-encoded.

cases.name: attack_apache_encoded_dot_traversal_uppercase
cases.note: Apache httpd CVE-2021-41773 and its incomplete-fix follow-up CVE-2021-42013. The same payload spelled with uppercase percent-hex.

cases.name: attack_apache_double_encoded_dot
cases.note: Apache httpd CVE-2021-41773 and its incomplete-fix follow-up CVE-2021-42013. CVE-2021-42013 bypassed the first fix by encoding the '%' itself: '%%32%65' decodes to '%2e' and then to '.'.

cases.name: attack_jetty_encoded_dot_segment
cases.note: Eclipse Jetty CVE-2021-28164 and CVE-2021-34429 (ambiguous paths reach WEB-INF). CVE-2021-28164's payload: an encoded '.' segment that the security constraint did not see but the file lookup did.

cases.name: attack_jetty_u_escape_dot
cases.note: Eclipse Jetty CVE-2021-28164 and CVE-2021-34429 (ambiguous paths reach WEB-INF). CVE-2021-34429's '%u002e', a non-standard 16-bit escape some parsers accept. Here '%u0' is not two hex digits, so it denies.

cases.name: attack_jetty_encoded_nul_segment
cases.note: Eclipse Jetty CVE-2021-28164 and CVE-2021-34429 (ambiguous paths reach WEB-INF). CVE-2021-34429's other payload: an encoded NUL ends the string for a C-level consumer but not for the Java one.

cases.name: attack_dot_dot_slash_slash
cases.note: swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings, 'Directory Traversal' (Intruder/traversals-8-deep-exotic-encoding.txt), the same list SecLists carries as LFI fuzzing input. '....//' survives a filter that deletes one '../' and leaves '../' behind.

cases.name: attack_dot_dot_dot_slash
cases.note: swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings, 'Directory Traversal' (Intruder/traversals-8-deep-exotic-encoding.txt), the same list SecLists carries as LFI fuzzing input. '.../' and './' mixed so a one-pass filter leaves a real dot segment.

cases.name: attack_double_encoded_dot_dot
cases.note: swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings, 'Directory Traversal' (Intruder/traversals-8-deep-exotic-encoding.txt), the same list SecLists carries as LFI fuzzing input. Double encoding: '%252e' decodes to '%2e' and then to '.', so a proxy that decodes once and a back end that decodes twice disagree.

cases.name: attack_triple_encoded_dot_dot
cases.note: swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings, 'Directory Traversal' (Intruder/traversals-8-deep-exotic-encoding.txt), the same list SecLists carries as LFI fuzzing input. Triple encoding, for a chain with three decoders in it.

cases.name: attack_double_encoded_slash
cases.note: swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings, 'Directory Traversal' (Intruder/traversals-8-deep-exotic-encoding.txt), the same list SecLists carries as LFI fuzzing input. Double-encoded separator.

cases.name: attack_fully_encoded_traversal
cases.note: swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings, 'Directory Traversal' (Intruder/traversals-8-deep-exotic-encoding.txt), the same list SecLists carries as LFI fuzzing input. Every byte of '../' encoded.

cases.name: attack_mixed_encoded_traversal
cases.note: swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings, 'Directory Traversal' (Intruder/traversals-8-deep-exotic-encoding.txt), the same list SecLists carries as LFI fuzzing input. One dot plain, one encoded, separator encoded.

cases.name: attack_overlong_slash_lowercase
cases.note: IIS MS00-078 / CVE-2000-0884, the 'Unicode' directory traversal, and the overlong-UTF-8 section of PayloadsAllTheThings 'Directory Traversal'. %C0%AF is an overlong encoding of '/', %C0%AE of '.', %C1%9C of '\' and %C0%80 of NUL; a decoder that does not reject overlong forms turns them back into those ASCII bytes. The original payload, in the lowercase hex it is always published in, which denies for its hex case before the overlong form matters.

cases.name: attack_overlong_slash_uppercase
cases.note: IIS MS00-078 / CVE-2000-0884, the 'Unicode' directory traversal, and the overlong-UTF-8 section of PayloadsAllTheThings 'Directory Traversal'. %C0%AF is an overlong encoding of '/', %C0%AE of '.', %C1%9C of '\' and %C0%80 of NUL; a decoder that does not reject overlong forms turns them back into those ASCII bytes. DENIED since the path's decoded bytes must be well-formed UTF-8: 0xC0 can never start a sequence, so the overlong '/' is rejected whatever its hex case.

cases.name: attack_overlong_dot_lowercase
cases.note: IIS MS00-078 / CVE-2000-0884, the 'Unicode' directory traversal, and the overlong-UTF-8 section of PayloadsAllTheThings 'Directory Traversal'. %C0%AF is an overlong encoding of '/', %C0%AE of '.', %C1%9C of '\' and %C0%80 of NUL; a decoder that does not reject overlong forms turns them back into those ASCII bytes. An overlong '..' segment, lowercase.

cases.name: attack_overlong_dot_uppercase
cases.note: IIS MS00-078 / CVE-2000-0884, the 'Unicode' directory traversal, and the overlong-UTF-8 section of PayloadsAllTheThings 'Directory Traversal'. %C0%AF is an overlong encoding of '/', %C0%AE of '.', %C1%9C of '\' and %C0%80 of NUL; a decoder that does not reject overlong forms turns them back into those ASCII bytes. DENIED: an overlong '..' segment. The dot-segment rule never sees it (the segment is four percent-escapes, not '..'), but the UTF-8 rule rejects every 0xC0 lead byte.

cases.name: attack_overlong_backslash_uppercase
cases.note: IIS MS00-078 / CVE-2000-0884, the 'Unicode' directory traversal, and the overlong-UTF-8 section of PayloadsAllTheThings 'Directory Traversal'. %C0%AF is an overlong encoding of '/', %C0%AE of '.', %C1%9C of '\' and %C0%80 of NUL; a decoder that does not reject overlong forms turns them back into those ASCII bytes. DENIED: %C1%9C is an overlong '\', which a server reading '\' as a separator would resolve. 0xC1 is the other lead byte no well-formed sequence can start with.

cases.name: attack_overlong_nul
cases.note: IIS MS00-078 / CVE-2000-0884, the 'Unicode' directory traversal, and the overlong-UTF-8 section of PayloadsAllTheThings 'Directory Traversal'. %C0%AF is an overlong encoding of '/', %C0%AE of '.', %C1%9C of '\' and %C0%80 of NUL; a decoder that does not reject overlong forms turns them back into those ASCII bytes. DENIED: %C0%80 is an overlong NUL. A plain %00 denies as an encoded control byte, and this spelling of the same byte now denies too.

cases.name: attack_overlong_slash_three_byte
cases.note: The rule is the WHATWG Encoding standard's UTF-8 decoder (https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/#utf-8-decoder), not a list of bad bytes, because a list is only ever the payloads someone has already seen. The same overlong '/' as the %C0%AF payload, written in three bytes. Its lead byte 0xE0 is a perfectly ordinary one, so a rule that just banned 0xC0 and 0xC1 would let this through; the decoder denies it because 0xE0 requires its first continuation byte to be at least 0xA0.

cases.name: attack_overlong_slash_four_byte
cases.note: The rule is the WHATWG Encoding standard's UTF-8 decoder (https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/#utf-8-decoder), not a list of bad bytes, because a list is only ever the payloads someone has already seen. The same overlong '/' again, in four bytes. Lead byte 0xF0 is ordinary too; the decoder denies it because 0xF0 requires its first continuation byte to be at least 0x90.

cases.name: attack_lone_surrogate
cases.note: The rule is the WHATWG Encoding standard's UTF-8 decoder (https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/#utf-8-decoder), not a list of bad bytes, because a list is only ever the payloads someone has already seen. U+D800, a lone high surrogate. UTF-8 cannot carry surrogates at all (RFC 3629 section 3), and a decoder that emits one hands the layers above it a string that can be re-encoded several ways. The decoder denies it because 0xED caps its first continuation byte at 0x9F.

cases.name: attack_lead_byte_above_the_last_code_point
cases.note: The rule is the WHATWG Encoding standard's UTF-8 decoder (https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/#utf-8-decoder), not a list of bad bytes, because a list is only ever the payloads someone has already seen. 0xF5 and above could only encode a code point past U+10FFFF, which does not exist, so no well-formed sequence starts with one.

cases.name: attack_truncated_utf8_sequence
cases.note: The rule is the WHATWG Encoding standard's UTF-8 decoder (https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/#utf-8-decoder), not a list of bad bytes, because a list is only ever the payloads someone has already seen. A three-byte sequence the path ends one byte into. A decoder that ignores the end of its input may pad or drop the missing byte, and two decoders that guess differently read one path as two. A half-finished sequence at the end of the path is denied.

cases.name: attack_accepted_well_formed_non_ascii
cases.note: Not an attack: the floor the rule above must not cross. 'ete' with two e-acutes, properly encoded, is ACCEPTED and kept byte for byte. Without a case like this the UTF-8 rule could be satisfied by denying every non-ASCII path, which would be a different and much blunter rule.

cases.name: attack_accepted_well_formed_four_byte
cases.note: Not an attack: the same floor for a four-byte sequence (U+1F512, a padlock). ACCEPTED. It shares its lead byte 0xF0 with attack_overlong_slash_four_byte and differs only in the continuation bytes, which is exactly what the decoder's boundaries look at.

cases.name: attack_accepted_fullwidth_solidus
cases.note: The full-width and look-alike section of PayloadsAllTheThings 'Directory Traversal' (%uff0e / %uff0f / %u2215): U+FF0F FULLWIDTH SOLIDUS, U+FF0E FULLWIDTH FULL STOP and U+2215 DIVISION SLASH are mapped to ASCII '/' and '.' by best-fit character mapping in some stacks. ACCEPTED as UTF-8 percent-escapes (U+FF0F is EF BC 8F). Kept encoded; a best-fit mapping would read it as '/'.

cases.name: attack_accepted_fullwidth_full_stop
cases.note: The full-width and look-alike section of PayloadsAllTheThings 'Directory Traversal' (%uff0e / %uff0f / %u2215): U+FF0F FULLWIDTH SOLIDUS, U+FF0E FULLWIDTH FULL STOP and U+2215 DIVISION SLASH are mapped to ASCII '/' and '.' by best-fit character mapping in some stacks. ACCEPTED (U+FF0E is EF BC 8E), a full-width '..' segment.

cases.name: attack_accepted_division_slash
cases.note: The full-width and look-alike section of PayloadsAllTheThings 'Directory Traversal' (%uff0e / %uff0f / %u2215): U+FF0F FULLWIDTH SOLIDUS, U+FF0E FULLWIDTH FULL STOP and U+2215 DIVISION SLASH are mapped to ASCII '/' and '.' by best-fit character mapping in some stacks. ACCEPTED (U+2215 is E2 88 95).

cases.name: attack_fullwidth_solidus_lowercase
cases.note: The full-width and look-alike section of PayloadsAllTheThings 'Directory Traversal' (%uff0e / %uff0f / %u2215): U+FF0F FULLWIDTH SOLIDUS, U+FF0E FULLWIDTH FULL STOP and U+2215 DIVISION SLASH are mapped to ASCII '/' and '.' by best-fit character mapping in some stacks. The same bytes in lowercase hex deny, so the two spellings can never both be targets.

cases.name: attack_fullwidth_solidus_raw
cases.note: The full-width and look-alike section of PayloadsAllTheThings 'Directory Traversal' (%uff0e / %uff0f / %u2215): U+FF0F FULLWIDTH SOLIDUS, U+FF0E FULLWIDTH FULL STOP and U+2215 DIVISION SLASH are mapped to ASCII '/' and '.' by best-fit character mapping in some stacks. The same character sent raw rather than percent-encoded: a non-ASCII byte in a path denies.

cases.name: attack_unicode_u_escape_solidus
cases.note: The full-width and look-alike section of PayloadsAllTheThings 'Directory Traversal' (%uff0e / %uff0f / %u2215): U+FF0F FULLWIDTH SOLIDUS, U+FF0E FULLWIDTH FULL STOP and U+2215 DIVISION SLASH are mapped to ASCII '/' and '.' by best-fit character mapping in some stacks. The non-standard '%u2215' 16-bit escape form.

cases.name: attack_nul_encoded_truncation
cases.note: Null-byte and control-character truncation, on every path-traversal payload list (PayloadsAllTheThings 'Directory Traversal', and Jetty CVE-2021-34429 for the '.%00' form). '%00' truncates the path for a C-level consumer and does not for a Java or Go one, so the two see different files.

cases.name: attack_nul_raw_truncation
cases.note: Null-byte and control-character truncation, on every path-traversal payload list (PayloadsAllTheThings 'Directory Traversal', and Jetty CVE-2021-34429 for the '.%00' form). The same byte sent raw.

cases.name: attack_del_control
cases.note: Null-byte and control-character truncation, on every path-traversal payload list (PayloadsAllTheThings 'Directory Traversal', and Jetty CVE-2021-34429 for the '.%00' form). An encoded DEL (0x7F).

cases.name: attack_vertical_tab_encoded
cases.note: Null-byte and control-character truncation, on every path-traversal payload list (PayloadsAllTheThings 'Directory Traversal', and Jetty CVE-2021-34429 for the '.%00' form). An encoded vertical tab, which some servers strip as whitespace.

cases.name: attack_tab_raw
cases.note: Null-byte and control-character truncation, on every path-traversal payload list (PayloadsAllTheThings 'Directory Traversal', and Jetty CVE-2021-34429 for the '.%00' form). A raw tab inside the target: some servers reject it, some treat it as the end of the target, some pass it through.

cases.name: attack_crlf_raw_in_path
cases.note: CRLF / response-splitting injection, OWASP 'CRLF Injection' and the HTTP Garden's finding that origin servers disagree about stray CR and LF in a request (Kallus et al., 'The HTTP Garden', arXiv:2405.17737). A raw CRLF in the target.

cases.name: attack_crlf_encoded_in_path
cases.note: CRLF / response-splitting injection, OWASP 'CRLF Injection' and the HTTP Garden's finding that origin servers disagree about stray CR and LF in a request (Kallus et al., 'The HTTP Garden', arXiv:2405.17737). The encoded form, which a component that decodes before forwarding turns back into a real CRLF.

cases.name: attack_crlf_in_authority
cases.note: CRLF / response-splitting injection, OWASP 'CRLF Injection' and the HTTP Garden's finding that origin servers disagree about stray CR and LF in a request (Kallus et al., 'The HTTP Garden', arXiv:2405.17737). The same injection in the authority.

cases.name: attack_crlf_in_method
cases.note: CRLF / response-splitting injection, OWASP 'CRLF Injection' and the HTTP Garden's finding that origin servers disagree about stray CR and LF in a request (Kallus et al., 'The HTTP Garden', arXiv:2405.17737). The same injection in the method.

cases.name: attack_lf_in_scheme
cases.note: CRLF / response-splitting injection, OWASP 'CRLF Injection' and the HTTP Garden's finding that origin servers disagree about stray CR and LF in a request (Kallus et al., 'The HTTP Garden', arXiv:2405.17737). A stray LF in the scheme.

cases.name: attack_absolute_form_other_host
cases.note: RFC 9112 3.2's four request-target forms, and the HTTP Garden's observation that servers disagree about which forms they accept and how they rewrite them (Kallus et al., arXiv:2405.17737). Absolute-form carrying a second, different authority. An adapter must deny when two copies of the authority disagree; if one ever reaches the canonicalizer as a path, it denies here too.

cases.name: attack_absolute_form_same_host
cases.note: RFC 9112 3.2's four request-target forms, and the HTTP Garden's observation that servers disagree about which forms they accept and how they rewrite them (Kallus et al., arXiv:2405.17737). Absolute-form naming the same host: still not a path.

cases.name: attack_authority_form_target
cases.note: RFC 9112 3.2's four request-target forms, and the HTTP Garden's observation that servers disagree about which forms they accept and how they rewrite them (Kallus et al., arXiv:2405.17737). Authority-form, which only CONNECT may use.

cases.name: attack_protocol_relative_target
cases.note: RFC 9112 3.2's four request-target forms, and the HTTP Garden's observation that servers disagree about which forms they accept and how they rewrite them (Kallus et al., arXiv:2405.17737). '//host/path' is read as a network-path reference by RFC 3986 and as a path by many servers.

cases.name: attack_backslash_authority_confusion
cases.note: RFC 9112 3.2's four request-target forms, and the HTTP Garden's observation that servers disagree about which forms they accept and how they rewrite them (Kallus et al., arXiv:2405.17737). '/\evil.com/' is read as '//evil.com/' by browsers and the WHATWG URL Standard, and as a path by most servers.

cases.name: attack_accepted_at_sign_in_path
cases.note: RFC 9112 3.2's four request-target forms, and the HTTP Garden's observation that servers disagree about which forms they accept and how they rewrite them (Kallus et al., arXiv:2405.17737). ACCEPTED: '@' is an ordinary path byte (RFC 3986 pchar), so this is one path under example.com and nothing else. It is here because the authority-confusion shape '/@host/' is a common payload; the userinfo rule denies '@' in the authority, which is where it would be dangerous.

cases.name: attack_host_duplicate_joined_by_comma
cases.note: Host-header attacks: PortSwigger 'HTTP Host header attacks' and OWASP 'Host Header Injection'. RFC 9112 3.3 makes the Host field value the target URI's authority, so anything ambiguous there denies. Two Host headers joined the way a field list is joined: the front end reads the first, the back end the last.

cases.name: attack_host_duplicate_joined_by_space
cases.note: Host-header attacks: PortSwigger 'HTTP Host header attacks' and OWASP 'Host Header Injection'. RFC 9112 3.3 makes the Host field value the target URI's authority, so anything ambiguous there denies. The same duplicate, joined by a space.

cases.name: attack_host_userinfo_prefix
cases.note: Host-header attacks: PortSwigger 'HTTP Host header attacks' and OWASP 'Host Header Injection'. RFC 9112 3.3 makes the Host field value the target URI's authority, so anything ambiguous there denies. 'a@b': everything before '@' is userinfo, so a parser that keeps it reads the host as evil.com and one that drops it reads example.com.

cases.name: attack_host_userinfo_suffix
cases.note: Host-header attacks: PortSwigger 'HTTP Host header attacks' and OWASP 'Host Header Injection'. RFC 9112 3.3 makes the Host field value the target URI's authority, so anything ambiguous there denies. The same trick the other way round.

cases.name: attack_host_tab_suffix
cases.note: Host-header attacks: PortSwigger 'HTTP Host header attacks' and OWASP 'Host Header Injection'. RFC 9112 3.3 makes the Host field value the target URI's authority, so anything ambiguous there denies. A trailing tab, which some servers strip and some keep.

cases.name: attack_host_leading_space
cases.note: Host-header attacks: PortSwigger 'HTTP Host header attacks' and OWASP 'Host Header Injection'. RFC 9112 3.3 makes the Host field value the target URI's authority, so anything ambiguous there denies. Leading whitespace.

cases.name: attack_host_nul
cases.note: Host-header attacks: PortSwigger 'HTTP Host header attacks' and OWASP 'Host Header Injection'. RFC 9112 3.3 makes the Host field value the target URI's authority, so anything ambiguous there denies. A NUL in the host truncates it for a C-level resolver.

cases.name: attack_host_encoded_dot
cases.note: Host-header attacks: PortSwigger 'HTTP Host header attacks' and OWASP 'Host Header Injection'. RFC 9112 3.3 makes the Host field value the target URI's authority, so anything ambiguous there denies. Percent-encoding in the authority: a component that decodes it sees example.com, one that does not sees a name with a literal '%'.

cases.name: attack_host_bracketed_name
cases.note: Host-header attacks: PortSwigger 'HTTP Host header attacks' and OWASP 'Host Header Injection'. RFC 9112 3.3 makes the Host field value the target URI's authority, so anything ambiguous there denies. Brackets around a name, which only an IPv6 literal may use.

cases.name: attack_host_uppercase_punycode
cases.note: Host-header attacks: PortSwigger 'HTTP Host header attacks' and OWASP 'Host Header Injection'. RFC 9112 3.3 makes the Host field value the target URI's authority, so anything ambiguous there denies. Punycode written in uppercase. Folding it would be a merge, so it denies; the lowercase spelling is accepted (see attack_accepted_homoglyph_punycode).

cases.name: attack_host_raw_homoglyph
cases.note: Host-header attacks: PortSwigger 'HTTP Host header attacks' and OWASP 'Host Header Injection'. RFC 9112 3.3 makes the Host field value the target URI's authority, so anything ambiguous there denies. A Cyrillic small letter a (U+0430) in place of the ASCII 'a'. Sent raw, it is non-ASCII and denies: an international name must arrive as punycode.

cases.name: attack_accepted_homoglyph_punycode
cases.note: Host-header attacks: PortSwigger 'HTTP Host header attacks' and OWASP 'Host Header Injection'. RFC 9112 3.3 makes the Host field value the target URI's authority, so anything ambiguous there denies. ACCEPTED: the punycode of the Cyrillic look-alike above. It is a different name from example.com and gets a different target, which is the right answer; punycode is the only spelling that reaches the wire.

cases.name: attack_host_octal_loopback
cases.note: SSRF host-encoding lists (PayloadsAllTheThings 'Server Side Request Forgery', and the WHATWG URL Standard's 'ends in a number' rule). inet_aton reads a leading-zero part as octal, so 0177.0.0.1 is 127.0.0.1 to a C resolver and a name to DNS.

cases.name: attack_host_padded_dotted_quad
cases.note: SSRF host-encoding lists: zero-padded octets, read as octal by inet_aton.

cases.name: attack_host_name_ending_in_number
cases.note: WHATWG URL Standard 'ends in a number' checker: a name whose last label is all digits is parsed as an IPv4 address by browsers and as a name by DNS.

cases.name: attack_host_ipv6_uncompressed_mapped_ipv4
cases.note: RFC 5952 4: an IPv4-mapped address written the long way. Only the one RFC 5952 spelling is accepted.

cases.name: attack_accepted_ipv6_mapped_loopback
cases.note: RFC 5952 4. ACCEPTED: this is the one canonical spelling of the IPv4-mapped loopback, so it is kept. The dotted spelling of the same address, [::ffff:127.0.0.1], denies (see host_ipv6_embedded_ipv4), which is a split, not a merge: one address has one accepted target and one rejected spelling.

cases.name: attack_port_plus_sign
cases.note: RFC 3986 3.2.3 and RFC 9110 4.2.3. A port a parser reads differently from the next parser is a different destination. A leading '+', which some integer parsers accept.

cases.name: attack_port_whitespace
cases.note: RFC 3986 3.2.3 and RFC 9110 4.2.3. A port a parser reads differently from the next parser is a different destination. Whitespace around the port.

cases.name: attack_port_fullwidth_digits
cases.note: RFC 3986 3.2.3 and RFC 9110 4.2.3. A port a parser reads differently from the next parser is a different destination. Full-width digits, which a best-fit mapping would turn into 8443.

cases.name: attack_port_huge
cases.note: RFC 3986 3.2.3 and RFC 9110 4.2.3. A port a parser reads differently from the next parser is a different destination. A port past 16 bits, which wraps in a parser that truncates: 65536+8443 is 8443 modulo 65536.

cases.name: attack_method_smuggled_request_line
cases.note: RFC 9110 9.1 (methods are case-sensitive) and 5.6.2 (a method is a token); the HTTP Garden reports origin servers that accept non-token bytes in the method (Kallus et al., arXiv:2405.17737). A whole request line handed over as the method by a confused adapter.

cases.name: attack_method_nul
cases.note: RFC 9110 9.1 (methods are case-sensitive) and 5.6.2 (a method is a token); the HTTP Garden reports origin servers that accept non-token bytes in the method (Kallus et al., arXiv:2405.17737). A NUL after the method.

cases.name: attack_method_override_tunnel
cases.note: RFC 9110 9.1 (methods are case-sensitive) and 5.6.2 (a method is a token); the HTTP Garden reports origin servers that accept non-token bytes in the method (Kallus et al., arXiv:2405.17737). A second method smuggled after a separator, the shape of an X-HTTP-Method-Override tunnel.

cases.name: attack_accepted_trailing_dot_in_path
cases.note: IIS / Windows file-name handling, on every web-shell and source-disclosure payload list: Windows strips trailing dots and spaces from a name, NTFS exposes a file's default data stream as 'name::$DATA', and 8.3 short names (ADMIN~1) reach the same file as the long name. ACCEPTED: a trailing '.' inside a segment is an ordinary character (only a whole '.' segment denies). On Windows this reaches the same file as /admin.

cases.name: attack_accepted_trailing_dots_in_path
cases.note: IIS / Windows file-name handling, on every web-shell and source-disclosure payload list: Windows strips trailing dots and spaces from a name, NTFS exposes a file's default data stream as 'name::$DATA', and 8.3 short names (ADMIN~1) reach the same file as the long name. ACCEPTED, same family, three dots.

cases.name: attack_accepted_trailing_encoded_space
cases.note: IIS / Windows file-name handling, on every web-shell and source-disclosure payload list: Windows strips trailing dots and spaces from a name, NTFS exposes a file's default data stream as 'name::$DATA', and 8.3 short names (ADMIN~1) reach the same file as the long name. ACCEPTED: an encoded trailing space, which Windows strips.

cases.name: attack_accepted_ntfs_data_stream
cases.note: IIS / Windows file-name handling, on every web-shell and source-disclosure payload list: Windows strips trailing dots and spaces from a name, NTFS exposes a file's default data stream as 'name::$DATA', and 8.3 short names (ADMIN~1) reach the same file as the long name. ACCEPTED: ':' and '$' are ordinary path bytes (RFC 3986 pchar), so the classic '::$DATA' source-disclosure suffix passes through unchanged.

cases.name: attack_accepted_short_file_name
cases.note: IIS / Windows file-name handling, on every web-shell and source-disclosure payload list: Windows strips trailing dots and spaces from a name, NTFS exposes a file's default data stream as 'name::$DATA', and 8.3 short names (ADMIN~1) reach the same file as the long name. ACCEPTED: an 8.3 short name. Path case is kept exactly, so this is a different target from /administrator, which is the safe direction.

cases.name: attack_traversal_at_the_path_limit
cases.note: A 4096-byte traversal payload, exactly at the path limit, so the dot-segment rule is what denies it. Its pair below is one repetition longer.

cases.name: attack_traversal_over_the_path_limit
cases.note: The same payload one repetition longer (4099 bytes). It denies for the length, not for its dot segments: limits are checked before any field is read, so the intended reason cannot be pinned past the limit. The pair above pins it.

cases.name: attack_accepted_ipv4_unspecified
cases.note: SSRF host lists (PayloadsAllTheThings 'Server Side Request Forgery', the 'localhost bypass' section): the unspecified address reaches a service bound to every interface, so it is a common stand-in for 127.0.0.1. ACCEPTED: 0.0.0.0 is a dotted quad, the one IPv4 spelling every parser reads the same way, so it is a perfectly canonical host and gets its own target. The canonicalizer decides spelling, never reachability; which hosts a deployment may talk to is the caveat set's job.

cases.name: attack_accepted_ipv6_unspecified
cases.note: SSRF host lists (PayloadsAllTheThings 'Server Side Request Forgery', the 'localhost bypass' section): the unspecified address reaches a service bound to every interface, so it is a common stand-in for 127.0.0.1. ACCEPTED: '::' is the RFC 5952 spelling of the IPv6 unspecified address, so it is kept. Same judgement as the case above.
